reference.title: Lying Frog Crunch Feet Together (male)
reference.listing: Video; data sheet: body part Waist, equipment Body weight, exercise type Strength

breathing.pattern: Exhale as you curl up, inhale as you lower.
breathing.cadence: About 1 s up, a short squeeze, about 1.5 s down

prescription.tempo: About 1 s up, brief pause, 1.5-2 s down
prescription.progression: Slower lowering and a 2 s hold, then arms overhead

cues.text: Lie on your back, bring the soles of the feet together close to the hips and let the knees fall out to the sides. Fingertips lightly behind the head, elbows wide.
Breathe out and curl the head, shoulders and shoulder blades off the mat; ribs toward the hips.
Short squeeze at the top. Knees stay open and relaxed; low back stays on the mat.
Breathe in and lower slowly, shoulder blades first, head last.
Rest the head briefly; repeat without bouncing.

mistakes.mistake: Squeezing the knees up and together as you curl
mistakes.fix: Leave the legs relaxed in the frog position; only the trunk moves.

mistakes.mistake: Arching the low back to start the curl
mistakes.fix: Exhale and draw the ribs down first.

kinematics.measure: Upper trunk (T12 to C7) from the floor
kinematics.norm: Shoulder blades clear the mat as in a crunch (clinical opinion)
Small: about 3 degrees of lumbar flexion in a crunch, cited by Escamilla 2016 from earlier work
Most of the curl happens here (clinical opinion)
Soles together, knees out; the legs stay still (clinical opinion)
Hands support the head only; elbows stay wide (clinical opinion)
Controlled, about 1 s up and 1.5-2 s down (clinical opinion)

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.

Low-back pain, disc problems or flexion intolerance: start with a McGill-style curl-up, dead bug or plank; partial curl-ups gave the best abdominal challenge for the least spine compression in one model study (Axler and McGill 1997).
Hip or groin pain in the frog position: move the feet further from the hips or use a pillow under each knee.
Pregnancy and postpartum (diastasis recti): get individual guidance before dynamic trunk-flexion work.
Osteoporosis or vertebral fracture: avoid repeated loaded spinal flexion and twisting.
The athlete mesh rests on the mat; the rig collision shapes are thicker than the mesh at the back and buttocks, so floorTolerance records how far those proxy shapes sink below the mat surface.
modify: Neck pain: cross the arms on the chest.
Tight hips: feet further away, knees less open.
regressions: Smaller range: head and shoulders only.
progressions: Slow 3 s lowering with a 2 s hold.

muscleNotes.core: Rectus abdominis curls the ribs toward the pelvis exactly as in a crunch (about 53% upper and 39% lower rectus MVIC, Escamilla 2016). The legs only change the base.
muscleNotes.obliques_r: Assist the curl and keep the trunk square (about 28-33% MVIC in a crunch, Escamilla 2016).
muscleNotes.obliques_l: Assist the curl and keep the trunk square (about 28-33% MVIC in a crunch, Escamilla 2016).
muscleNotes.adductors_r: Lengthened with the knees out; they rest, which is why the frog position is used to take the legs out of the movement (clinical opinion). Hip flexors stay quiet in pure trunk-flexion work (Andersson 1997).
muscleNotes.adductors_l: Lengthened with the knees out; they rest, which is why the frog position is used to take the legs out of the movement (clinical opinion). Hip flexors stay quiet in pure trunk-flexion work (Andersson 1997).
